idiom_name: application-defined struct subject + one convert function per credential mechanism
implementation_notes: C has no identity type in the standard library, so the descriptor is a plain struct - a stable subject id plus the attributes consumers need (roles as a string table or bitmask, tenant, authentication method) - filled once by a per-mechanism convert function and read through accessor functions. The conversion is where the credential format lives: a PAM-based service fills the id with pam_get_user(3) / pam_get_item(3, PAM_USER) and then resolves roles, while a local peer can be described from the kernel-verified struct ucred that getsockopt(SO_PEERCRED) returns. Copy every string you keep - PAM and the kernel own their buffers - and treat the struct as const after the boundary; the classic OO shape (an abstract descriptor with interchangeable implementations) is only justified when mechanisms must be pluggable at run time.
pitfalls: The pointers PAM hands out (pam_get_user, pam_get_item) must not be freed or modified and become invalid after pam_end - copy the subject id into storage the descriptor owns.

SO_PEERCRED credentials are only trustworthy for connected AF_UNIX peers and are captured at connect time; pid and uid can be recycled later, so treat them as an attestation of the peer, not as a lifetime guarantee.
A descriptor whose strings point into request-scoped buffers dangles once the request ends; ownership of every attribute must be explicit.
